function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

function.description:
Search your long-term memory of past conversations, or browse recent sessions. This is your recall -- every past session is searchable, and this tool summarizes what happened.

TWO MODES:
1. Recent sessions (no query): Call with no arguments to see what was worked on recently. Returns titles, previews, and timestamps. Zero LLM cost, instant. Start here when the user asks what were we working on or what did we do recently.
2. Keyword search (with query): Search for specific topics across all past sessions. Returns LLM-generated summaries of matching sessions.

USE THIS PROACTIVELY when:
- The user says 'we did this before', 'remember when', 'last time', 'as I mentioned'
- The user asks about a topic you worked on before but don't have in current context
- The user references a project, person, or concept that seems familiar but isn't in memory
- You want to check if you've solved a similar problem before
- The user asks 'what did we do about X?' or 'how did we fix Y?'

Don't hesitate to search when it is actually cross-session -- it's fast and cheap. Better to search and confirm than to guess or ask the user to repeat themselves.

Search syntax: keywords joined with OR for broad recall (elevenlabs OR baseten OR funding), phrases for exact match ("docker networking"), boolean (python NOT java), prefix (deploy*). IMPORTANT: Use OR between keywords for best results — FTS5 defaults to AND which misses sessions that only mention some terms. If a broad OR query returns nothing, try individual keyword searches in parallel. Returns summaries of the top matching sessions.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

{"content": "   230|Bob sometimes wonders what his father felt, whether he knew, in some wordless way, that we were building more than toy airplanes. Whether he understood that the real project was the son standing beside him, learning to trust his own competence, preparing to row out into waters his father would never navigate. The garage door still opened on those evenings, spilling light into the suburban dark, the smell of sawdust and oil drifting out like incense. Inside, two people bent to their work, passing time together in the shared language of making, building something that would outlast them both. The belief that transformation was possible. That raw materials could become beautiful. That the right combination of knowledge and effort could create things that that mattered.
   231|
   232|**Transition: From Wood to Stars**
   233|
   234|The skills learned in that garage—the patience to measure twice, the courage to fail and rebuild, the understanding that invisible forces could be harnessed to do extraordinary things—would soon find an outlet far beyond anything Bob could have imagined. The Space Race had begun, and a boy who had learned to models and troubleshoot radios was about to discover that his hands could help build something that would reach for the stars themselves.
   235|
   236|## Chapter 5: The Spark Ignites
   237|
   238|### The TV Repair Shop
   239|
   240|The summer before tenth grade, Bob's father announced that it was time for his son to learn what work actually meant. Not the abstract work of school assignments, not the project work of the garage, but the clock-punching, customer-serving, money-earning work that occupied the majority of adult life. He had arranged a job for Bob at Hendricks TV & Electronics, a small repair shop that smelled of solder flux and ozone and the particular mustiness of vacuum tubes past their prime.  Mr. Hendricks was a bald man with perpetually cigarette -stained fingers and a habit of talking to himself while he worked. He took one look at the fifteen-year-old standing in his doorway and said, "Can you solder?"-"Yes, sir."-"Show me." Bob spent the next ten minutes demonstrating what he knew—how to tin an iron, how to heat the joint rather than the solder, how to create that bright, concave fillet that meant a good connection. Mr. Hendricks watched without comment, then handed him a basket of vacuum tubes. "Test these. The checker is in the back. Write down which ones are bad. When you're done, sweep the floor, your hired. After that, we'll see about teaching you something." The job paid $1.25 an hour, minimum wage, but what it offered in education was worth far more. Bob spent that summer and the two that followed driving around town doing pickup and delivery with a older worker and learning the applied electronics that would form the foundation of his career. He learned to read schematic diagrams, those intricate maps of electron flow that turned abstract symbols into working circuits. He learned to trace signals through televisions and radios, to identify failure points by symptom, to repair rather than replace because customers couldn't afford new sets.
   241|
   242|Soon after he encountered his first computer—not in the shop, but through his school . Dr. Richardson taught mathematics Bob noticed the man carried a textbook titled *Introduction to Digital Computers*. "You interested in that sort of thing?" Dr. Richardson asked, watching Bob eye the book. "I don't really know what it is, sir. I've read about them in magazines."
   243|
   244|"Come by the sometime. I'll show you our machine. It's not much—an IBM 1620 used for payroll —but it's a real computer. We program it on weekends when it is not being used. Make it do calculations, process data, solve problems. It's like having a very fast, very stupid assistant that follows instructions perfectly." Bob went the following Saturday. The computer filled a room, cabinets of transistors and magnetic core memory, spinning tape drives that sounded like sewing machines on amphetamines. Dr. Richardson showed him how to punch cards, how to write simple programs in raw assembly code, how the machine translated human instructions into the binary language of on-off switches and gates that was all the hardware understood.
   245|
   246|"This is the future” -. "Everything is going to change. Transportation, communication, manufacturing. You want to be part of that change; you need to understand these machines." That afternoon, Bob decided he would be an electrical engineer. Not a decision made in isolation. He wanted to work with these machines, these thinking engines that were transforming the world. He wanted to understand capabilities that had not been imagined yet. Yet the room sized computer of that time had a ten thousand time less compute than a modern mobile phone.
   247|
   248|### The First Car
   249|
   250|Bobs first car was a Chrysler valiant. It was blue, and had a mind of its own. The heater only worked when it wanted to, which in Michigan meant I spent most of the winter driving with my windows cracked to keep the windshield from fogging up. The manual gear shift had a mind of its own, sometimes finding third when he was reaching for first, sometimes refusing to find any gear at all until I'd pumped the clutch three times. Bobs parents bought it with the arrangement that Bob would pay it back. Bob earned the money to buy it, working weekends at a local TV and radio repair shop. It represented something more than transportation—it represented independence, achievement, the first tangible evidence that Bob could provide for himself. Bob remembered driving to the lake with his friends, the wind their hair, the radio blasting whatever station they could pick up. They had no destination in the strictest sense—they just drove. They followed roads they’d never taken, discovered places they’d never known existed, pulled over at random diners to eat french fries and just lived life.
   251|
   252|### High School Engineering
   253|
   254|Bob's high school didn't offer computer classes—they barely had functioning typewriters—but it did have a physics teacher named Mr. Kovacs who recognized something in the quiet student who sat in the front row and asked questions that went beyond the curriculum. "You're the TV shop kid, right?." - "I work there, yes, sir."-"You ever think about science fair?" Bob hadn't. Science fair was for the rich kids, the ones who built volcanoes or grew mold in petri dishes. But Mr. Kovacs explained that engineering projects were different, that Bob could build something real, something that demonstrated understanding of principles.
   255|
   256|That winter, Bob designed and built an analog weather computer—not a digital machine like the IBM 1620, but a system of operational amplifiers and potentiometers that could solve differential equations. It was crude, limited, built from salvaged parts and vacuum tubes that glowed orange in the dim basement where he assembled it. But it worked. You could set up an equation, adjust the coefficients with dial switches, and watch the solution trace across an oscilloscope screen. The project won the regional science fair. More importantly, it won Bob a scholarship—a small one, not enough to cover everything, but enough to make college possible. 
   257|
   258|### The Weight of Expectation
   259|
   260|College acceptance brought new pressures. Bob was going to be the first in his family to attend university—a milestone that carried both opportunity and obligation. His father and mother and for that matter the rest of the neighborhood could not visualize anyone going to college at first. One of the adult neighbors told Bob he was wasting his time no one from this neighborhood has the money or class to be a college student. His mother was quieter about it, but Bob could see the worry in her eyes. She understood something his father didn't: that education changed people, that the boy who went away might not be the same man who returned. She was proud, deeply proud, but also afraid of losing him to a world she didn't understand. "Don't forget who you are," she told him the night before he left for campus. "Don't forget where you came from. The world you're entering—it has different values than ours. Money matters more there. Status matters more. Don't let them convince you that we're simple or stupid because we didn't go to college. Your father and I did the best we could with what we had." Bob promised, not fully understanding what he was promising. He was eighteen, eager to escape the constraints of his upbringing, hungry for the knowledge and experiences that awaited him. The caution his mother offered felt like a weight he didn't want to carry.
   261|
   262|### Walk About
   263|
   264|There's something about walking—really walking, for hours on end—that changes the way you think about the world. It's not exercise. It's not transportation. It's a different way of being in the world, a slower pace that lets your mind catch up with your body.
   265|
   266|When I was nineteen, I took a walk about. Not the Australian kind, where you walk through the Outback and come face to face with your own mortality. I mean the American kind, where you just... go.  Bob gathered a couple of guy friends, and they just started walking starting in a Lake Michigan beach town and with back back in hand the started following the coast north. For six days they walked until they reached a place where the sand dunes disappeared into the water and they could go no further. They walked through beach’s, over sand dunes and through farmland. It was cathartic.
   267|
   268|### Michigan State University
   269|
   270|At the time the Vietnam war raged on and in his senior year of high school Bob received a low draft number in the national draft lottery. This meant he was bound for combat in the rice patties of Vietnam. I few days later he received a letter from a government agency, they needed electronics technicians and offered Bob an alternative, a small scholarship and relief from the draft in exchange for occasional work overseas. Bob discussed this with his father who had a very practical view. He said, “If you’re given an opportunity to serve your country in a way less likely to get you killed take it.” So Bob did, that is another story for another time.
   271|
   272|After high school Bob went to community college because he could live home and work earning enough for tuition. Bob enrolled at Michigan State University in the following fall, choosing it over the University of Michigan because of a spring high school college visit.  Bob and a friend first went to the University of Michigan, the rushed between buildings  and were totally convinced that it was the best choice. The next weekend his friend said “ let’s check out Michigan State “ Bob was convinced that the University of Michigan was the best choice bet went because of his friend. They spent the morning with a tour that convinced Bob that Michigan State was a good second choice but…  Then by lunch the tour was over and Bob and his friend sat by the river in a beautiful garden scape and 2 co-Ed’s sat down by them and so Bob picked Michigan State. It is strange how small effects can change the direction of your life. When he started Michigan State there were students from backgrounds he couldn't comprehend. There were kids from wealthy families who talked about summers in Europe, who drove sports cars their parents had bought them, who treated education as an entitlement rather than a privilege. Bob’s parents didn’t have the money to help much. Bob arrived with a single suitcase, a slide rule his father had given him and his bicycle, and just enough in savings from his TV shop wages to cover the first semester. He worked in the physics lab to cover his room and board and at night repairing TVs . The scholarship covered a little of tuition, but nothing else—He learned to live lean, to make do, to stretch resources the way his mother had taught him. The coursework was demanding in ways that high school hadn't prepared him for. Physics and calculus consumed hours each day, problem sets that needed not just calculation but genuine understanding of underlying principles. Bob discovered that he had gaps in his preparation—his community college hadn't covered some topics and he ... [truncated]
   273|
   274|### The Computer Revolution Accelerates
   275|
   276|By Bob's sophomore year, the world was changing faster than the curriculum could keep up. Integrated circuits were replacing vacuum tubes, shrinking computers from room-sized mainframes to machines that sat on desks. The university acquired a PDP-8, a minicomputer that students could actually touch, program, learn from. Bob spent time he could not spare in the computer center. He learned assembly language, then higher-level languages as they emerged. He wrote programs that solved engineering problems, that simulated physical systems, that demonstrated principles he was learning in his other classes. The computer became a tool for understanding, a way to explore ideas that would have been impossibly time-consuming to work through by hand. He also saw the commercial potential. Companies were desperate for people who understood both hardware and software, who could bridge the gap between the physical systems being designed and the digital control systems that would run them. 
   277|
   278|### Fermilab
   279|
   280|The opportunity that would shape Bob's future came unexpectedly. A professor Bob worked for mentioned that his work at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Chicago was looking for student engineers to help develop his experiments. The pay was good—and the experience would be unlike anything available on campus. Bob applied without expecting much. He was an undergraduate, after all, competing against graduate students for a position at one of the premier physics research facilities in the world. But his practical experience counted for something. The interviewers were less interested in his grades than in his ability to produce results, to understand systems from the component level up. He got the job. The summer after his junior year, Bob moved to a small apartment in Batavia, Illinois, and reported to work at a facility that looked like something from science fiction. The main accelerator ring was four miles in circumference, buried underground, a tunnel of superconducting magnets and particle detectors that probed the fundamental structure of matter.
   281|
   282|His job was more prosaic but no less important. The systems he developed, built from discrete transistors, and early integrated circuits and 40 tons of iron plate measured the energy of subatomic particles that existed for an unimaginably short time. Bob spent his days tracing signals through schematics, replacing components, redesigning subsystems. He worked alongside physicists and graduate students who were trying to understand the universe who respected Bob for his practical ability to make things that worked. The experience was transformative in ways that classroom education couldn't be. At Fermilab, the stakes were real. When a control system failed, the accelerator shut down, and every hour of downtime cost thousands of dollars in lost research time. Bob learned to work under pressure, to diagnose problems quickly, to implement fixes that would hold. He learned to communicate with scientists who spoke a different language, to translate between the abstract goals of physics and the concrete constraints of engineering. He also learned that he was good at this—really good. The physicists sought his opinion on design decisions. The physicists requested him specifically when their equipment malfunctioned. He was, still an undergraduate, and he was contributing meaningfully to one of the most advanced scientific facilities in the world. The summer ended too quickly. Bob returned to Michigan State for his senior year with new confidence, new skills, and new clarity about what he wanted to do. He didn't want to be a physicist—he respected the science, but his talents lay in building the tools that made science possible. He wanted to design systems, create infrastructure, solve the practical problems that enabled others to push the boundaries of knowledge. More immediately, he wanted to return to Fermilab. The experience had been too valuable to be a one-time thing. He talked to his supervisors about returning after graduation, about making the temporary summer positi... [truncated]
   283|
   284|### The Departure
   285|
   286|The decision to leave Michigan after graduation carried emotional weight that Bob hadn't expected. He had spent his life in one town, in the orbit of his family, within reach of the garage and the kitchen and the familiar rhythms of home. Moving meant distance—not just physical, but the beginning of a separation that would only widen as he built his own life.
   287|
   288|His father was proud but quiet about the Fermilab opportunity. He had always imagined his son becoming an engineer, but the reality of it—Bob leaving, building a career in a world his father couldn't fully comprehend—brought a melancholy that he didn't know how to express. The garage had been their shared language, but Bob was learning new languages now, entering realms where his father's ability couldn't follow. His mother was more direct about her feelings. She cried when they said goodbye, then wiped her eyes.
   289|
   290|### The Road Ahead
   291|
   292|Bob arrived at Fermilab in June, a newly minted graduate with a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering and two summer's worth of experience that had already proven he could do the work. The lab had grown in the year since he'd been there—new buildings, new equipment, new staff drawn from universities around the world. The main accelerator was running at higher energies, probing deeper into the structure of matter, generating data that would reshape physics. And Bob was part of it. Not in the spotlight—he would never be the physicist making discoveries or writing papers that changed how humanity understood the universe. But in the essential background. It was enough.
   293|
   294|
   295|# Part Three: The Particle and The Person
   296|
   297|## Chapter 6: Life as an Engineer 
   298|
   299|*Finding love in the space between atoms*
   300|
   301|### The Graduate Engineer
   302|
   303|Fermilab in 1970 was a place of contradictions—a frontier outpost of pure science planted in the cornfields west of Chicago, where the world's most sophisticated technology coexisted with rural Illinois practicality. The main accelerator ring tunneled beneath farmland that had been cornfields just a few years before. Physicists in tweed jackets walked past equipment sheds where local farmers stored their harvest equipment. The frontier between cutting-edge research and agricultural tradition ran through every aspect of daily life.
   304|
   305|Bob arrived, fresh from graduation, carrying everything he owned in a used car with 120,000 miles on the odometer. His apartment in Batavia was small—one bedroom, kitchenette, bathroom the size of a closet—but it was his, paid for with his own salary.
   306|
   307|The work was everything he had hoped for and more challenging than he had expected. Fermilab's control systems were a patchwork of technologies—some state-of-the-art, some obsolete the day they were installed, all needing to work together with absolute reliability. A particle accelerator is a delicate instrument. The beam travels at nearly the speed of light through a vacuum pipe surrounded by superconducting magnets operating at temperatures near absolute zero. Thousands of sensors monitor every parameter, and the control systems Bob worked on had to process this data in real time, making adjustments faster than human operators could react.
